resources.string: How mast cells release stored signals
An educational model of adult human tissues. Cell sizes, granule counts and timing are schematic, not measurements or personal data.

Mature mast cells live in tissues. Examples include connective tissue in the skin and near the linings of airways and the intestine. They often sit near small blood vessels. The highlights identify separate sites, not a route between them.
A mast cell keeps many small granules in its cytoplasm. These compartments hold substances the cell can release locally.
When the mast cell is activated, some granules can fuse with its surface and release stored substances into the surrounding tissue. This is called degranulation.
Released substances spread around the mast cell and can affect nearby cells and small blood vessels. The mast cell stays in the tissue beside the vessel.

How helper T cells coordinate a response
An educational model of adult human immunity. Cell sizes, signal symbols and timing are schematic, not measurements or personal data.
A helper T cell can become active after receiving cues from a neighboring immune cell. This is the start of the coordination shown here.
An active helper T cell can release chemical messages called cytokines. They can influence what other immune cells do.
Here, a B cell and another T cell illustrate two kinds of cells that can receive help. The branching motion shows who can receive messages, not fixed paths through tissue.
Help can support an antibody response by B cells or strengthen the activity of other T cells. Different helper T cells can support different responses.

How cytotoxic T cells act on an abnormal cell
An educational model of adult human immunity. Cell shapes, contact and timing are schematic, not measurements or personal data. Shape alone does not identify an abnormal cell.
An active cytotoxic T cell can recognize some abnormal human cells. The illustrated target is a cell of the body; its different shape only identifies it in this drawing.
The cytotoxic T cell comes into close contact with the target. The highlighted boundary shows where the two cells meet.
The target begins controlled cell death
The interaction can start a controlled process in the target called apoptosis. Here the target draws inward and develops small bulges, two changes that can occur during apoptosis.
The cytotoxic T cell can move away as the target continues to break down. The neighboring cell shown here stays intact.

How regulatory T cells moderate a response
An educational model of adult human immunity. Cell shapes are schematic. The moving band symbolizes activity and represents no measurements, time scale or personal data.
Several immune cells are already responding in this tissue. The moving band stands for their shared activity.
A regulatory T cell acts near other immune cells. Immune responses can be regulated while they are still underway.
Regulatory T cells can restrain excess activity in other immune cells. The band narrows to show a weaker response; the responding cells are still present.
Moderation does not mean switching off the immune system. Keeping activity in check helps protect the body’s own tissues without ending all immune activity.
